title: ‘The Life of a Composer’
content:
Via Marcin Wichary, who writes:

Designer Pablo Stanley created a really fun interactive exploration of what it takes to create a seemingly simple “composer” (industry’s jargon for a more sophisticated input field or things like it). [...]

Also, I am burying the lede: it’s a really enjoyable and well-crafted experience — don’t miss the sound and music! — and this unique way of talking about interface details could be inspiring in and of itself.

You can also watch the entire thing as a video with Stanley narrating, but I personally liked the interactive version more.

At first I enjoyed this a lot. I got maybe a quarter of the way through it before I thought it was too long — and then poked around and figured out that I wasn’t even halfway done with it yet. At first, yes, it brings to life just how many details a designer might have to think about. But after a bit it’s just interminable neuroticism. I drew this conclusion before I looked up where Stanley works, which I would have won a bet on. I wound up skipping over half of it, which makes this a rare exception — I almost never link to anything on DF which I skipped through.

At the point where I began wondering if this whole thing was a prank of some sort, all I could think was: this is why platforms need a HIG; why the HIG needs to be thorough, thoughtful, and good; and why designers ought to follow the platform’s HIG. It takes humility to defer to a standard platform reference, and humility is what is lacking in much of modern UI design in general, and Stanley’s interactive essay in particular.

And is it really industry jargon to call these “composers”? It’s a text box. It needs some buttons. It ought to look good. Its functionality ought to be obvious. It shouldn’t be needlessly distracting. Get to work. Build that. Move on. If you call these “composers” you might be in a segment of the industry where the life of a designer is so abstract and proudly navel-gazing that you don’t just lose the forest for the trees, but you lose the trees for endless rumination about the texture of bark. Real designers stay focused on helping users get through a delightful forest.

 ★

New York vs auto-enshittification (permalink)

As of February 27, 2027, it will be illegal for companies in New York to charge car-owners a subscription fee or an upcharge for any software feature that runs on hardware already installed in their car. It's a bold – if imperfect – disenshittification gambit aimed at the extremely (and increasingly) enshittified automotive industry:

https://wgna.com/car-bill-extra-fees/

In a state of nature, there'd be no reason to pass a law like this. Say BMW decided to sell you a car that charged you a monthly subscription for the "feature" that auto-dipped your high-beams when there was an oncoming car (a thing BMW actually does):

https://www.autoevolution.com/news/netizens-up-in-arms-over-bmw-adaptive-headlight-subscription-237335.html

In a state of nature, BMW's sleazy scam would conjure forth competitors who would offer mechanics and drivers a one-click way to unlock the feature forever. Drivers would curse BMW and pay a one-time fee to get permanent access to the feature, and that would be the end of the matter. Indeed, the fact that this third-party fix could exist at all might well convince BMW not to bother with the high-beam scam in the first place (and if it didn't, well, then tinkerers, hackers, and entrepreneurs would swiftly obviate it).

But we don't live in a state of nature. We live in a world with a federal "anticircumvention" law: Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA 1201), which imposes a 5-year sentence and a $500k fine for this kind of reverse engineering, even if it does not result in a copyright infringement.

There's no copyright law that says you can't change the software in your car to activate your high-beams' automatic controller, but that doesn't matter, because activating the controller without BMW's permission requires a reverse-engineering step and that's a felony.

Jay Freeman rightly calls this "felony contempt of business model" because it lets companies send you to literal prison for doing otherwise legal things, just because it makes them unhappy.

What's more, copyright is a firmly federal matter: copyright law "pre-empts" the states, meaning that states can't pass laws that modify federal copyright policy. That means that states can't override DMCA 1201 by legalizing reverse-engineering for otherwise lawful purposes (such as independent repair, performing software upgrades, or allowing generic consumables and parts).

Anticircumvention is an attractive nuisance: it invites manufacturers to dream up as many scams as they can think of and then bury them in their products, secure in the knowledge that it is a literal felony to thwart their commercial plans. It's especially bad for cars, where anticircumvention is used:

  • to block third-party parts and independent repair;

  • to prevent drivers from preventing manufacturers, lenders and dealerships from spying on their driving habits, car informatics, and locations;

  • to enable lenders (and hackers who break into dealerships' computers) to immobilize your car without any notice, appeal or due process:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/24/rent-to-pwn/#kitt-is-a-demon

The New York State bill (S.9348A/A.10411A) partially addresses some of these unfair and deceptive practices:

https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/S9348/amendment/A

Before I get into what this law does (and doesn't) do, I want to get into how it does anything at all. Remember: anticircumvention was shoehorned into copyright law, and copyright is a federal matter. Copyright enjoys pre-emption, a ban on states' modifying it.

At first blush, it seems like the states shouldn't be able to do anything about the enshittification that anticircumvention law enables. But the Right to Repair movement came up with a clever hack around pre-emption. States can't override federal copyright law, but state legislatures can regulate goods and services that are sold within their states. That means that states can simply ban the sale of goods that use anticircumvention to rip off or spy on the people who live within state limits.

This is the basis for several successful Right to Repair laws, starting in 2022 with Colorado's powered wheelchair repair law (HB22-1031, cosponsored by the very excellent Brianna Titone):

https://pluralistic.net/2022/06/08/chair-ish/#r2r

This law does not purport to limit which copyrights the private-equity-backed powered wheelchair duopoly can exercise. It just orders anyone selling powered wheelchairs in Colorado to take steps to enable independent repair such that these copyright issues (including anticircumvention) never arise.

This became the template for a slew of state repair bills, including Oregon's electronics repair law, which was later copy/pasted into Washington state law:

https://pirg.org/oregon/updates/governor-kotek-signs-the-right-to-repair-act-into-law/

A very similar law was passed in New York state, only to be gutted by Governor Kathy Hochul:

https://www.techdirt.com/2024/02/07/nys-right-to-repair-law-was-neutered-by-lobbyists-and-governor-hochul-after-passage-now-some-lawmakers-are-trying-to-fix-it/

Hochul will shortly get a chance to redeem herself, when A8405, a law that re-inserts all the provisions she stripped out of the original repair law, comes to her desk:

https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/bills/2025/A8405

Perhaps Hochul will sign that law. After all, her press release about the new automotive bill sure makes it sound like she's anti-enshittification:

My message to car companies is clear: this kind of deceptive business model isn’t going to fly in New York State. Keep your hands out of New Yorkers’ wallets.

https://www.governor.ny.gov/news/money-your-pockets-governor-hochul-signs-bill-restricting-exploitative-vehicle-subscription

But the specifics of this new NY automotive bill matter, and they're a decidedly mixed bag. Let's start with the penalty for noncompliance: a dealer, automotive manufacturer or lender who violates the new law faces a whopping $250 fine per violation. That means that if your dealer charges you $1,000 for a software upgrade and you later realize you've been ripped off, they'll only pay a penalty of $250.

In this case, a dealer who manages to fleece one driver for every three who know their rights and can figure out how to enforce them will still come out ahead – and that's only if you can get the dealer to refund your $1000, which might involve going to small claims court.

Then there's the carve-outs: this law does not cover subscription fees and software upsells for "navigation system updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, in-vehicle wi-fi, telematics services, roadside assistance, software-dependent driver assistance or driver automation features, or vehicle-connected services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation."

This is a huge loophole. Take that last clause, "services that rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." This clause allows manufacturers to bypass the entire statute, merely by redesigning their subscription and software upsells to "rely on cellular or other data networks for continued operation." For example, the BMW feature that automatically dips your high-beams could "require" a daily check for new versions and then the company can claim that the feature relies "on cellular or other data networks for continued operation."

Sure, a judge might eventually find that "continued operation" doesn't mean a daily check for software updates, but only after the state AG or a class action lawyer forces the question, which could take years. Also: don't hold your breath waiting for the class action lawyer, because the car manufacturers can also make you click through a binding arbitration waiver when you first turn on your car and thus take away your right to join a class action:

https://pluralistic.net/2025/10/27/shit-shack/#binding-arbitration

Beyond this, there's the breadth of vague phrases like "driver automation features" (is automatically dipping your high-beams a "driver automation feature?" I could sure see a lawyer making that argument). Likewise "telematics" (a buzzword that might mean anything, nothing or everything).

On the other hand, there are some interesting ambiguities in this bill that I quite like. For example: if you live in New Jersey, but you happen to be in New York on the day Tesla bills you for subscribing to your whole battery (some Tesla models only let you use half your battery's charge unless you pay a monthly fee). Does that mean Tesla violated the law by charging a fee for a subscription feature for a car that is in the state of New York? That would be a fun one to see!

Like I said, this is only a partial fix for auto-enshittification. It won't stop your car from spying on you and ratting you out to your insurer:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/03/12/market-failure/#car-wars

It won't help you if the manufacturer goes bust and bricks your car:

https://pluralistic.net/2024/10/10/software-based-car/#based

It won't help you if Tesla hacks your odometer to sell a lie about the range you can expect from your charge:

https://pluralistic.net/2023/07/28/edison-not-tesla/#demon-haunted-world

This law would have had much more effect if it was better-drafted; on the other hand, maybe if it was drafted to capture a more meaningful slice of enshittificatory gambits, Hochul would have gutted it the way she did with the state's 2022 electronics repair bill.

Above all, though, we must remember: the only reason this bill exists at all is that Congress created DMCA 1201, the "felony contempt of business-model" law that lets companies conjure new crimes out of thin air and send you to prison for making their shareholders sad.

It's fantastic that the Repair Coalition came up with a loophole that lets states protect the American public from some of the worst effects of anticircumvention law, and it's cool that this tactic is being used to fight other kinds of enshittification.

But none of this should be necessary at all, and the real fix is for Congress to repeal Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act.

title: Book Review: Slow Gods by Claire North ★★★★⯪
content:
Cor! This is a great big doorstop of a space opera. It perfectly co-opts the language of pulp sci-fi without becoming pulpy. If you've read plenty of sci-fi, you'll be familiar with some of the tropes and how the author has reinvented them. There are shades of Murderbot's autistic meltdowns, the living ships from Of Monsters and Mainframes, and a million other stories.

The book flips between genres effortlessly. You're reading a space-diplomacy novel, then you're in a battle, then there's this-Earth-emotion-you-call-love, then galactic politics, then you realise you're in a ghost story. It is episodic with plenty of great cliff-hangers. The cultures are sufficiently otherworldly and the plot feels sufficiently plausible.

One of the supposed "rules" of sci-fi is that no-one cares about your world building. You don't need to explain that the economy of Rigel Ⅶ is based on gibzits, nor should you go on an extended diversion about how FTL travel works in this universe. Claire North happily and wisely doesn't give a shit about these conventions and dedicates several blissful chapters to the intricacies of the universe. At times it feels like a pop-science history book for an alternate reality.

One particularly impressive chapter is about the plethora of pronouns scattered throughout the book. Perhaps it is a little bit satirical? Either way, it's an excellent look at how languages and cultures evolve. Similarly, Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the tepid response of some nations is given short shrift here.

A fun and fearsome read.

title: Covering a body with eight smaller copies of itself
content:
It’s obvious that you could cover a cube with smaller cubes. You could, for example, take a cube with side 1 and cover it a cube of side ½ centered on each corner.

It’s not as obvious how you would cover a ball with smaller balls, but you could cover the unit ball with balls of radius ½√3 centered at the points (±½, ±½, ±½).

In fact, you could cover a ball with four smaller balls [1].

Now consider an arbitrary convex shape K in three dimensions with non-empty interior. Is it possible to cover K by copies of itself? Since K has non-empty interior, you could cover K by putting a smaller version of K around every point. And if K is compact, then this cover has a finite subcover. But there might be a lot of elements in this finite cover. What’s the minimum number possible in general? It takes eight cubes to cover a cube, so the minimum is at least 8. But could some odd shape take more?

Hadwiger’s covering conjecture says that K can be covered by eight copies of itself. That is, there exists a scaling constant 0 < λ < 1 and shift vectors vi such that

Dror Aiger, Sariel Har-Peled, and Goran Žužić posted a proof of Hadwiger’s conjecture on arXiv yesterday. The abstract to their paper says “The proof was discovered using an experimental harness on top of Gemini 4 Carbon and formally verified in Lean 4.”

I’ve heard good things about the Google’s new Carbon model. This is the first announcement of a major theorem proved with the assistance of a Google model that I’ve noticed.

Related posts

  • Splitting a convex set through its center
  • Convex hull of zeros
  • Separation of Convex Sets in Linear Topological Spaces

[1] Inscribe the vertices of regular tetrahedron on the unit sphere, then multiply the vectors representing the vertices by ⅓. Center spheres of radius ⅔√2 at each vertex.

title: This Week in Source Control: 25 November 2026
content:
This week’s version control and forge news, gathered from release feeds for source control clients and forges, the Lobsters vcs tag, Hacker News, and my boosts on Mastodon. Package management news is in the Saturday This Week in Package Management roundup.

Scaling

Scaling horizontally: how we moved beyond Multi-Raft (Enroute) covers the 0.4.0 release of Enroute, a Git server that stores object data in S3 and one replicated log of refs and layers per repository. Under Multi-Raft every repository had its own Raft group with its own heartbeats and elections. At 2,048 concurrent writers across 100,000 repositories, late heartbeats set off thousands of elections and the 99th percentile push time reached 83 seconds.

The new design uses failover from Vertical Paxos: a single root log runs Raft and assigns a sequencer to each repository’s log, so timers and elections run only in the root log. The root log leader also places each repository’s three replicas in distinct zones. The protocol is checked with Stateright against the real implementation and with a Jepsen suite. At 300,000 repositories the team measured up to 24,000 pushes per second.

Accelerating development for massive Git repositories (The Android ABFS Team, Google Developers Blog) announces the open-sourcing of ABFS, the system Android uses for checkouts and builds. Android 17’s open source release has 1,084 Git repositories and 1.62 million files. A repo sync took around 36 minutes and a full build around 80.

ABFS replaces the checkout with CASFS, a Linux kernel filesystem that exposes Git object hashes as extended attributes and fetches file contents on first read. Server-side processes ingest Git objects from Gerrit into a content-addressable store. Ninja-go records which files each build step read and reuses cached results only when those files still match. Checkouts now take under 8 seconds and full builds just over 2 minutes, and a Bazel integration exists as a proof of concept.

Releases

delta 0.21.1 adds a TUI based on a fork of gitu. It can browse git diff, git show and git log output, stage directly from delta-rendered diffs including side-by-side view, fold diffs, and reorder and fixup commits from the log. A new min-width option switches side-by-side mode on or off depending on terminal width. 0.21.2 lets the TUI open terminal editors such as vim and emacs -nw, and shows when a submodule is dirty.

GitButler 0.23.5 is now on Flathub as an official, verified package. Pushing the rest of a stack after several of its branches have merged now succeeds, and loading a large project far behind its upstream no longer uses gigabytes of memory. The CLI adds but worktree recycle, which reuses a clean archived worktree, including its build output and dependencies, for a new branch.

gt 2.0.0 (bircni, Gitea Blog), the Gitea command-line client, comes just over two weeks after 1.0.0. Its flags now match gh’s, so gt pr merge accepts --squash, --subject and --body. --json now requires a field list, and absent values are always null. Logs of a failed Actions run dropped from about 46,800 tokens to about 11,600, because the output drops timestamps and --failed prints only the failed steps.

Commands now run with a GITEA_TOKEN that lacks the read:user scope, so a token limited to read:repository can clone through gt’s credential helper in CI. Keyring entries are stored under gitea-cli:HOST. Local extensions now run only if the executable is owned by the user or root and is not world-writable.

GitLab 19.6 makes Rapid Diffs generally available as the replacement for the classic merge request diff view. Diffs are rendered on the server and streamed to the browser, which cuts the time to the first file from about 4.5 seconds to 1.5. Fine-grained personal access tokens can now read more through the GraphQL API, including blame, CODEOWNERS validation and deploy keys. Every action taken through the GitLab MCP server now creates an audit event.

Also out: forges v0.4.0.

Security

Forgejo 17.0.2 and 15.0.12 are security releases. The fixes:

  • With the internal SSH server on SQLite, public keys were matched with a case-insensitive SQL LIKE. A crafted key matching a target user’s key case-insensitively could authenticate as that user through a custom client. Matching is now by exact fingerprint and key content.
  • The endpoint that sets a primary email address accepted unverified addresses. An external service using Forgejo for sign-in could be tricked into granting access to the wrong account.
  • Commit headers were accepted in any order, so a crafted commit could display an incorrect diff.
  • The /tree-list and /find endpoints listed a repository’s files to users who lacked code read access.
  • The /activities/feeds and /heatmap APIs returned data outside the limits of repository-scoped and public-only access tokens.

On 16 November malicious JavaScript was served through Optimizely Web to visitors of 178 organisations, Report URI found (Scott Helme). The attacker added code to the customer-written Project JavaScript field of each snippet, and the modified snippets were served from cdn.optimizely.com. The payload swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses and skimmed payment cards. It also stole cookies and screenshots. Report URI lists gitlab.com and about.gitlab.com among the affected sites.

GitHub

GitHub Desktop 3.7.0 supports more than one signed-in account on the same host. Each repository is associated with one account, which is used for clone, publish and other Git operations. Existing repositories are migrated to the account previously associated with them. On the web, the new dashboard has a Favorite repositories section that syncs with pinned repositories in GitHub Mobile, up to 25 across both.

gh v2.105.0 adds gh event listen, which subscribes to a pull request through Event Streams, covered last week, and prints each event as a line of JSON. By default it exits after the first event, and --count, --follow and --timeout change that. gh pr view, gh run watch and gh api now print a hint pointing to it in place of polling. It requires access to the Event Streams preview.

In the latest changes to the pull request Overview preview, a mergeable pull request with failed optional checks now shows as mergeable. Force-push entries in the activity link to the old and new commits, commit entries show timestamps, and resolved review threads collapse.

The GitHub Enterprise Server 3.23 release candidate adds OAuth app access tokens that expire after eight hours, with refresh tokens. Expiry is the default for new OAuth apps and opt-in for existing ones. Enterprise Live Migrations from Azure DevOps is generally available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. It syncs Git history, branches, tags and pull requests continuously until cutover, and converts branch policies to rulesets.

Security advisory permissions, in Saturday’s roundup, let custom repository roles manage and publish advisories, which previously required admin access. Seth Larson writes that the Python Security Response Team tested it in a private beta, and that several more PSRT members now take part in triage, work that had fallen to repository admins.

The microsoft/onnxruntime repository disappeared on 17 November, first noticed on Hacker News when CI pipelines started failing, and returns a 404 at the time of writing. The StableBuild blog reports that it was removed with no prior announcement. The PyPI packages were still available, but builds that fetched source or release files from GitHub failed.

Elsewhere

Codeberg posted a post-mortem of the 18 November domain suspension covered last week. NameSilo had placed codeberg.org on client hold over two abuse cases without contacting Codeberg. One was a 2022 report that Codeberg disputes, about a repository archived since 2023. The other was malware in an account created on 16 November, reported only to the registrar, not to Codeberg’s abuse address.

Codeberg removed both repositories and is evaluating offers from other registrars. It moved its nameservers from NameSilo to deSEC in July. A switch to its spare codeberg.eu domain would affect two-factor authentication and every existing Git remote, and Codeberg is working with Forgejo on multi-domain support.

Announcing jj-musubi (Bryan O’Sullivan) introduces jj-musubi, which syncs copies of a Jujutsu repository across machines each time jj snapshots the working copy. One machine runs a hub and the others exchange history with it over SSH. Each machine’s workspaces appear prefixed with its name, so jj diff -r devbox/agent-1@ shows another machine’s work. Temporary VMs can lease membership, and a repository whose lease is not renewed is forgotten.

Syncs leave the files in each working copy alone, so new history can arrive while a build runs. O’Sullivan started the project that became Sapling and Mononoke at Meta, and cites Sapling’s Commit Cloud as the model. Key properties of the sync protocol are proved in Lean, and tests compare the Rust code against the Lean model.

Jujutsu Primer (Ethan Lowman) introduces jj to Git users in a colocated repository. It covers changes and commits, revsets, automatic rebasing, conflicts, the op log, the squash workflow, bookmarks, and stacked pull requests.

TODOs JJ Style (Ben C) describes keeping a to-do list as empty jj changes with descriptions, rebased onto real work when started. A git.private-commits setting of description('private:*') excludes them from pushes.

Send links for next week to @andrewnez@mastodon.social.
description: Releases, advisories, and articles from across version control and forges

title: Have You Tried Using Your Agent?
content:
In 2025, I wrote down some thoughts on “AX”. My fear was that AX would end up becoming the top priority for people building software. (I’m not against AX, I would simply prefer a priority of constituencies where the human experience is top.)

So where are we today?

I feel like we’re building things that are increasingly accessible to robots while remaining inaccessible to people.

And I’m nervous that the collective posture of technologists towards this trend is not, “We should make this more accessible to our fellow humans.” But rather, “Humans should use their agents to access our thing.”

In other words: instead of making things for each other, we’re spending our time and attention making things for machines.

“Is it accessible?” sometimes feels as though it colloquially means, “Can an AI agent access it?” And since the agent’s work is purportedly on our behalf, making something accessible to a machine counts as making it accessible to a human.

I’m afraid of conversations by software makers increasingly going like this:

“Are we ready to ship? Does it work for the AI?”

“Yes — but you can’t really use it yourself.”

“That’s ok, ship it. We can always fix that later — but also, who even does things themselves anymore? lol.”

I’m nervous of my interactions with organizations increasingly being along the lines of, “Your thing isn’t working for me.” And their default response being, “Did you try using your AI agent?”

We already built a world that increasingly sidelines people without smartphones. My parents struggle with everything from flying, to using grocery store coupons, to verifying their identity because they don’t have a smartphone.

In another 10-20 years, will the same be true but with AI agents?

The question, “Have you tried downloading our app?” will transform into, “Have you tried using your agent with ours?”

title: Has Jevons paradox broken down?
content:
On a recent YC podcast, Ramp's CEO Eric Glyman claimed that "over the last two months, Jevons paradox broke". Ramp is a corporate card and spend management company, so they see what tens of thousands of businesses actually spend on tokens - and growth in that spend went from 42% in July to 1.5% across August and September combined. Jevons paradox is the idea that making something cheaper makes people use so much more of it that total spend goes up.

Ramp's data certainly isn't the full story. It's inherently noisy, skews towards venture-backed tech companies, and won't capture spend that never touches Ramp - e.g. big contracts paid directly by bank transfer, or tokens bought through a cloud provider.

I've been thinking a lot about this recently, noticing that my token consumption has at best plateaued recently. I think there's a few core drivers for that, plus some organisational issues I'm noticing.

Why my own usage has stalled

Perhaps I'm in the minority, but I'm finding myself running out of stuff to actually build, at least on a personal level. I've built prototypes of a decade of random ideas I've had, most of them not quite as good in the flesh as I thought they'd be.

On a more professional level, there's plenty to build... but I'm very cognisant of "featureitis"[1]. I (still) believe saying no to features is a really key competitive advantage.

The final point I'd make is that I'm pretty exhausted from the increased pace of development. I used to have weeks to mull product and technical strategy while implementation was underway. In many cases this is now down to hours.

One strategy I've found that works quite well is capping myself at one hour a day of kicking off "new" stuff, and spending the rest of the day reviewing what comes back. That hour generates more than enough to fill the day - which means it's my attention, not the models, limiting how many tokens I get through.

Simon Willison spoke about this when coding agents started getting good, and I feel like the adrenaline of the excitement is wearing off. I've seen a lot of people I know get pretty ill from working themselves too hard, and I think we really need to focus on burnout prevention for people managing product and engineering decisions.

Everything feels disposable

In parallel to this, given the models have got so good recently, I find myself treating all software as pretty disposable mentally. It turns out the grind of getting something working and the related dopamine hit had a lot to do with staying motivated on ideas.

When you see models do weeks or months of hard software engineering work in minutes or hours, it's absolutely magical the first few times. But increasingly I've thrown models at previously impossibly ambitious projects [2] and it all seems so easy I find myself thinking everything is disposable in my head, which is a shame because there is still an awful lot to be said for the refinement and iteration phase after the initial prototyping.

But at least for personal itches I want to scratch, without that initial grind it's hard for me to stay focused on "finishing" a project. I'm sure those who have a similar inherent urge to build stuff can look at a graveyard of projects in their GitHub account.

The four steps of AI adoption

Tinkerers like me are in the vast minority of the overall population. But according to Ramp, the top 1% of spenders are 80% of all token spend - so if the heavy users are hitting limits, that shows up in the numbers. So it is interesting to hypothesise about how far people can go with this kind of stuff, because I think it sets some overall limits on token consumption per person.

To step back, I think there are 4 clear steps of AI adoption.

1. LLM chat. Occasional chatting with LLMs. Most, but certainly not all (yes, some organisations still do not have even basic LLM chat rolled out!) businesses are at around this stage. This is usually very token light - a few thousand tokens, with a few turns per conversation. Call it 50K tokens a day per person.

2. Ad hoc agents. A sizeable minority - but not a majority in my estimation - of organisations are moving towards agentic workflows (e.g. Claude Cowork). Software engineering tends to be far ahead of this, with most organisations adopting Claude Code et al, but outside of SWE adoption is still really lagging, often roadblocked on access control. An agent re-reads its whole context on every tool call, so even one session a day is around 3M tokens - my median Claude Code session is 2.6M.

3. Engineered agents. Defined autonomous agents executing long running, repeatable business processes, triggered manually. In software engineering this is becoming increasingly common, with many developers building systems that allow them to take a task and execute it with little to no handholding. Outside of SWE, this is vanishingly rare. I've only really seen startups do it. You can quickly get to 100s of millions of tokens a day.

4. Autonomous agents. The "end state" of sorts, which is agentic processes running autonomously in the business, spawning themselves and spawning other workflows (often recursively). You could think of this as a "software factory". What I'm more interested in though is this applied to non-SWE tasks, with entire business departments being able to be operated with a fleet of agents. This isn't really per person any more, but could easily be billions of tokens a day.

Therefore, I still think we have at least 4 orders of magnitude of token consumption to grow into.

So I don't think Jevons paradox has broken. Cheaper tokens get you more usage within a step, but moving up a step is an organisational problem, not a pricing one.

The intersection is what matters

But, given token prices are falling rapidly, and even faster per unit of intelligence, the real question seems to be does organisational change - and thus agentic system adoption and token consumption - outpace the decline in token costs? Glyman himself reckons the majority of spend on frontier models could be done by a simpler one.

It's still hard to say, but seeing how slowly, and let's be honest; badly, most organisations have adopted AI, it does make me question things. On the other side I do think there is enormous value to be created for agentic first startups to start tackling boring business processes, which may actually lead to this explosion of token consumption.

Also, there may be a limit to how efficient models can get, and therefore how far prices can fall. It's hard to say, but there's no doubt that video compression had staggering efficiency improvements in the late 90s, but quickly hit diminishing returns. I suspect that is the case with LLMs, but I've no idea if we are at the MPEG1 stage or H.264 stage.

I'd love to hear from you if you are having roadblocks (or not) implementing agentic workflows outside of SWE. I'm working on a piece on best practices for navigating this, and I'll treat all submissions strictly on background and confidential.

  1. A highly technical term for post AI products which have built thousands of features, turning the product into an absolute mess ↩︎

  2. For example, rewriting the entire ClickHouse query analyser and dispatch process to work on Vulkan - I don't know any shader code whatsoever - delivering orders of magnitude improvements in query speeds, or reverse engineering the Excel COM interface to work on Linux natively - when I haven't touched the Win32 API in decades, never mind reimplementing parts of it on Linux. ↩︎
description: Ramp's data shows growth in token spend stalling. Some thoughts on why my own token consumption has plateaued, and whether organisational change can outpace falling token prices.
